title: COVID-19 misinformation: Accuracy of articles about coronavirus prevention mostly shared on social media
screen_reason: Content analysis of the 30 most-shared online articles about COVID-19 prevention (Buzzsumo, April 2020). Two public-health experts judged each article accurate / misleading / inaccurate against WHO and CDC guidelines and the scientific literature: 6/30 (20%) misleading, 0 inaccurate. The paper also reports the share of all 4,904,160 social-media shares that went to misleading articles (36%). Both are quantitative shares with explicit denominators judged against external ground truth.

estimates.moderator_quote: We decided to identify 30 articles about prevention against coronavirus disease with the highest number of shares on social media (Facebook, Twitter, Pinterest, Reddit) using Buzzsumo, the online analytic tool.
estimates.notes: Headline CONTENT row. Denominator is items that exist in a rank-truncated single-topic keyword corpus, hence denom_scope=topical + denom_selection=curated. Coded CONTENT rather than QUALITY because the judgement is explicit guideline concordance stated as accurate/inaccurate, and a wholly accurate article could not receive the 'misleading' label (which by definition requires inaccurate content). None of the analyzed articles about coronavirus prevention was inaccurate according to the criteria."

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Table 1 gives per-subject splits (Medication 2 of 7 misleading; Masks 2 of 2; Hand washing 1 of 9; Surfaces cleaning 0 of 3; General 1 of 5; Isolation 1 of 4; etc.). Not extracted: these are topic subgroups within a single topical corpus, not country/platform/measure splits, the cell sizes are 1-9 articles, and Table 1 is internally inconsistent - the subject rows sum to 46 articles rather than 30 (the 'Other' category n=8 is also broken out into Contact lenses, Animals, Lifestyle and Alternative Medicine rows), 'Other' shows n=8 but only 1 misleading + 4 accurate = 5, and the Isolation row shows total shares 35,400 while listing 35,400 misleading plus 239,430 accurate shares. Table 1 therefore cannot support reliable sub-rows. 2) Source-type shares (29/30 = 97% non-affiliated websites; TV/radio 15/30 = 50%; peer-reviewed and official-institution websites 6.7% of articles) are provenance descriptions, not veracity shares, so no row. 3) '63% of social media users have shared news and information between each other' is cited from reference [3] (Schmidt et al.), not this paper's own data - excluded under R8. 4) No survey, exposure-log, reach or concentration data.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of a rank-truncated web corpus. Frame: Buzzsumo keyword search on 27 April 2020 ('coronavirus' OR 'COVID-19', each coupled with 'prevention'; 'SARS-CoV-2 prevention' dropped as <1% of results), no date restriction, retaining the 30 articles with the most social-media shares that contained some kind of preventive advice. n = 30 articles, 4,904,160 shares. No response rate applies. Coding: two independent researchers, both public-health experts, classified each article accurate / misleading / inaccurate against WHO or CDC guidelines or indexed scientific research; disagreements resolved by discussion or referral to an experienced epidemiologist. No inter-rater reliability statistic reported. Share counts are third-party (Buzzsumo) and the authors note they 'cannot rule out that it brought some unrecognizable bias into our study' and that they could not tell whether a sharer endorsed or warned against an article. Ethical approval not required. Very short observation window (one month, early pandemic), which matters because CDC/WHO mask guidance was itself changing during April 2020 - the ground truth is time-bound.
rob.item6_quote: We classified each article as either “accurate”, “misleading” or “inaccurate” using the following criteria: “accurate” publications had to be consistent with either the latest WHO or the Centers for Disease Prevention and Control (CDC) guidelines or results of scientific research available at: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science or Google Scholar. “Misleading” articles where those containing both accurate and inaccurate information while “inaccurate” had to contain information inconsistent with the guidelines or scientific knowledge sources.
rob.item10_quote: Out of the 30 top shared articles identified 24 were found to be accurate (80%) and 6 to be misleading (20%).
